title: Ephemeral lateral rail: compact rollout & cost quickcards for fast context
creator: Ava Chen
description: Problem: Engineers and PMs need rapid situational awareness about active rollouts and recent billing anomalies without leaving their current Console view. The current sidebar is dense; switching to full dashboard pages disrupts flow and increases time-to-action. Goal: Design an ephemeral lateral rail (a narrow, slide-in surface anchored to the right edge of the Console) that surfaces compact, actionable quickcards for: 1) active rollouts (canary status, error spikes, recent toggled routes) and 2) cost highlights (unexpected spend deltas, high-cost routes/models). The rail should be discoverable via keyboard shortcut, route-level quicklinks, and a persistent micro-chip in the top nav. It must be permission-aware (showing limited data to viewers) and dismissible without losing navigation state.
user_stories: As an ML infra engineer, I want a one-click view of the current canary rollout health for the model route I’m inspecting so I can decide whether to pause or rollback quickly.
As a product PM, I want to scan recent cost anomalies across my workspace without opening the full cost dashboard so I can flag follow-ups during standup.
As an on-call engineer, I want keyboard access to the lateral rail from any Console route so I can triage incidents faster.
As a viewer role user, I want the rail to hide sensitive cost details but still show high-level flags so we respect RBAC boundaries.
proposal_summary: Introduce an ephemeral right-side rail that slides over current content (not a full route change). The rail contains stacked quickcards: Rollout Summary card (canary %, success/error rate sparkline, recent deploy link, last 15m error rate), Cost Snapshot card (7d vs 30d delta, top 3 routes by spend), and Actions row (jump-to-deploy, open-eval, pin-to-dashboard). Cards are compact (60–120px height each), support progressive disclosure (expand to show traces or cost breakdown), and include lightweight CTA buttons for common workflows. The prototype uses motion to communicate ephemeral state and preserves the underlying URL/activity so developers can dismiss and resume work seamlessly.
accessibility_considerations: Ensure all interactive elements are focusable via keyboard; rail can be opened/closed with Cmd/Shift+K and Esc to close.
Provide ARIA live regions for status changes (e.g., canary failure alert) to notify screen reader users without requiring focus shift.
Contrast and size: quickcard typography meets AA for 14px text; critical badges use semantic colors and textual labels.
Respect reduced-motion preferences; provide a graceful opacity-based reveal instead of slide when reduced-motion is active.
analytics_and_metrics: Track open_rate of lateral rail (per user, per route)
Measure time_to_action after open (click to deploy/pause/rollback)
Monitor percent of opens that escalate to full dashboard navigations (to measure usefulness)
A/B test two densities: compact (2–3 cards) vs. dense (4–5 cards) for task completion speed and cognitive load
decisions: Use slide-over that does not change the primary route URL (keeps history stack clean).
Limit initial visible cards to Rollout Summary and Cost Snapshot; expansion controlled by user pinning.
Show aggregated cost bands to non-billing roles; exact spend numbers require billing permission.
open_questions: Should pinned quickcards persist across sessions or be workspace-scoped? (PM prefers workspace-scoped)
How granular should the RBAC rules be for cost numbers vs flags? (need security input)
What telemetry thresholds should trigger an auto-suggest to open the rail (e.g., sudden +30% spend delta)?
acceptance_criteria: Prototype validated in user testing with at least 6 engineers/PMs and average task completion improvement of 20% vs. baseline.
Design tokens and motion specs handed off to frontend with annotated Figma and accessibility notes.
RBAC matrix defined and implemented in mock data for frontend demos.
Telemetry events instrumented in the prototype for open_rate and time_to_action.
